A 2-day history of progressive right ring finger swelling and pain following a forceful jersey-pull injury during football. [THOUGHT]  
This is a classic presentation of “jersey finger”—a traumatic avulsion injury of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon from its insertion on the volar base of the distal phalanx. The mechanism (forceful hyperextension of a flexed finger during jersey-pull), affected digit (right ring finger—most commonly involved), and timeline (2-day progressive swelling and pain without skin breach or systemic signs) are highly characteristic. While tenosynovitis remains in the differential (hence the MRI/POCUS workup), the *lack* of classic inflammatory signs, combined with the specific mechanism and isolated DIP swelling, makes FDP avulsion far more likely. The X-ray showing soft tissue swelling at the DIP joint—without bony abnormality—is consistent with volar soft tissue hemorrhage/edema from tendon avulsion; subtle avulsion fragments may be missed on X-ray but are better assessed on MRI. - No reported skin breach (argues against inoculation-driven tenosynovitis).  
- Absence of systemic symptoms (e.g., fever, chills) and classic local signs of inflammation (erythema, warmth, stiffness) — inconsistent with acute pyogenic tenosynovitis.  
- Initial X-ray shows soft tissue swelling around the DIP joint without bony abnormality — typical appearance of acute FDP avulsion with hematoma/edema, often without visible avulsion fragment.  
- Clinical suspicion explicitly includes FDP tendon injury (avulsion/rupture) as a leading concern — corroborated by mechanism and anatomy.  
- MRI is indicated specifically to assess FDP tendon integrity, retraction, and bone attachment — aligning with diagnostic priority for jersey finger.

- MRI findings (tendon continuity, retraction distance, presence of avulsion fragment, sheath fluid) are pending — critical to confirm FDP avulsion vs. partial tear vs. other pathology.

- Clinical documentation of active and passive range of motion — specifically inability to actively flex the DIP joint (pathognomonic for FDP rupture) — is missing.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Jersey finger (flexor digitorum profundus tendon avulsion)
